sections.text: Two words you will meet a lot. A crate is the smallest unit of code the compiler builds at once. A package is a folder that Cargo manages; it holds one or more crates, plus a file called Cargo.toml that describes them.

There are two kinds of crate. A binary crate compiles to a program you can run, and it has a main function. A library crate has no main; it offers code for other crates to use. Every program in this course so far was a binary crate in a single file.
Run cargo new my_app and Cargo makes this package for you:

sections.code:
my_app/
    Cargo.toml        <- describes the package
    src/
        main.rs       <- the root of the binary crate
        lib.rs        <- (optional) the root of a library crate

sections.text: src/main.rs is the crate root of the binary, and src/lib.rs, if you add it, is the crate root of a library. The crate root is where the compiler starts reading, the same top-level module you met earlier. Cargo.toml looks like this:

The [package] part gives the name, the version and the Rust edition. The [dependencies] part lists the other crates you want. Here we ask for rand, a popular crate that makes random numbers. "0.10" means any compatible 0.10.x version. When you build, Cargo downloads rand from crates.io, the public place where people share crates, and builds it too. Then your code can write use rand::...; to use it. Cargo also writes a Cargo.lock file that records the exact versions, so everyone builds with the same ones.

Important: the editor in this app cannot download crates, and it compiles a single file with plain rustc, so there is no Cargo.toml here. Anything with a [dependencies] section is shown, not run. The standard library, std, is a crate that comes with Rust, so use std::... always works.
These are the Cargo commands you will use every day. Run them in a terminal, inside your package folder:

sections.code:
cargo new my_app      # make a new package
cargo build           # compile it
cargo run             # compile and run
cargo check           # check for errors, faster than build
cargo test            # run the tests (next lesson)
cargo add rand        # add a dependency to Cargo.toml
cargo build --release # compile with full optimizations

sections.text: Now back to modules. When a module grows, you move it to its own file. In src/main.rs, write mod garden; with a semicolon instead of a block. Rust then loads the module body from src/garden.rs. A module nested inside it, declared with pub mod vegetables; inside garden.rs, lives in src/garden/vegetables.rs.

The module tree is the same as if you had written everything inline. The paths in your code (garden::vegetables::count()) do not change, only where the text is stored. Here is the inline version, with comments showing where each part would live in files. It prints the same thing as the file version:

A package is like a project folder with a manifest file: Cargo.toml plays the role of package.json (npm) or requirements.txt plus setup (Python). crates.io is Rust's npm or PyPI. The crates you depend on are downloaded and compiled together with your code.

Coming from Java, Go or C#: a crate is roughly one compilation unit, like a Go module or a .NET assembly. A package can have one library crate and many binary crates (extra binaries go in src/bin/). Cargo.lock is committed for applications. Workspaces let several packages share one lock file and one build folder. The older layout garden/mod.rs also works, but garden.rs next to a garden/ folder is the current style.

exercise.prompt: Pretend the nested module is the file src/garden/vegetables.rs. Inside mod garden, add pub mod vegetables with a function pub fn count() -> u32 that returns 3. Then replace the 0 in main with garden::vegetables::count(). It should print: planted carrot, 3 in the garden

What does the [dependencies] section of Cargo.toml do?
options: Lists the crates your package needs, which Cargo downloads and builds
Lists the functions your package exports
Lists the files that the compiler should skip
